(CNN) -- Taliban advances in Pakistan are raising concerns in Islamabad and in capitals as far away as Washington. CNN senior international correspondent Nic Robertson examines how the Taliban has expanded its reach and what could be done to support Pakistan.

Students in burqas in Buner district.

How is the Taliban extending its influence in Pakistan?

The Taliban has significantly expanded its influence over the past several years, moving northward along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border from South Waziristan to North Waziristan, then to Bajur, and now across to Swat and Buner.

Its influence has also grown through links with several Punjab-based terrorist groups that have aligned themselves with the border Taliban and helped carry out attacks, including one on a police station in Lahore.

Since 2004-2005, the Pakistani government has been striking deals with various elements that were Taliban or later became Taliban. Those agreements have enabled the Taliban to expand its presence.

Is Pakistan going to fall or fail?

The overall answer is no. However, the Taliban is further destabilizing an already highly unstable situation. Pakistan has a weak government that faces challenges not only from the Taliban, but also from nearly every political party in the country.

It also faces pressure from across the border with its longstanding adversary, India, which means a large proportion of the Pakistani army remains tied up along that border rather than fighting terrorism.

The Taliban is not going to take Islamabad. However, its attacks and advances will weaken an already unstable government and make an already dangerous situation even more volatile. That, in turn, will allow the Taliban to wield more influence in the future than it does today.

What options are available to the Pakistani government and other countries?

Pakistan could form a broad-based government of national unity and seek greater international support, including financial aid and the lifting of trade restrictions, in order to strengthen the economy.

The international community could help Pakistan resolve its issues with India. This would support the economy, enable the government to focus on its internal problems, and allow it to exert greater influence over the situation in Afghanistan.

The Pakistani government would also need to convince its people that outside support and assistance are in their best interests as the country seeks to confront terrorism and stabilize itself.

To do so, the government would also have to win the support of its large Pashtun minority, from whom the Taliban draws much of its backing. That is difficult, particularly as the United States—which would need to be a principal supporter of Pakistan—continues to bomb targets in Pashtun areas, causing civilian casualties.
outputs.L2:
(CNN) — The Taliban’s gains inside Pakistan are causing alarm not only in Islamabad, but also in foreign capitals, including Washington. CNN senior international correspondent Nic Robertson examines the way the Taliban has expanded its reach and what measures might assist Pakistan. Students wearing burqas are seen in Buner district.

How is the Taliban increasing its presence in Pakistan?

Over the past several years, the Taliban has greatly widened its area of influence, pushing north along the Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier. Its reach has moved from South Waziristan into North Waziristan, then to Bajur, and now across into Swat and Buner.

Its influence has also grown because it has developed links with several terrorist organizations based in Punjab. These groups have aligned themselves with Taliban elements along the border and have helped carry out attacks, including an assault on a police station in Lahore.

Since around 2004 and 2005, Pakistan’s government has made agreements with various factions that either already belonged to the Taliban or later became part of it. Those arrangements have given the Taliban more room to expand.

Is Pakistan likely to collapse or be taken over?

In general, the answer is no. However, the Taliban is making an already highly unstable situation even more fragile.

Pakistan has a weak government under pressure not only from the Taliban, but also from nearly every political party in the country. It also faces tensions across the border with its longtime rival, India. Because of that, a significant portion of Pakistan’s army remains deployed along the Indian border instead of being used in counterterrorism operations.

The Taliban is not expected to seize Islamabad. Even so, its attacks and territorial gains are likely to further weaken a government that is already unstable and to make a dangerous situation still more unpredictable. As a result, the Taliban may be able to exercise greater influence in the future than it does now.

What choices are available to Pakistan and the international community?

Pakistan could create a broad national unity government and seek stronger backing from abroad. That support could include increased financial assistance and the removal of trade barriers to help strengthen the economy.

Other countries could also assist Pakistan in addressing its disputes with India. Progress on that front would benefit Pakistan’s economy, allow the government to concentrate more on domestic security problems, and improve its ability to affect developments in Afghanistan.

At the same time, Pakistan’s government would need to persuade its citizens that outside assistance serves their interests by helping fight terrorism and stabilize the country. To succeed, the government would also need to gain the confidence of its large Pashtun minority, a community from which the Taliban receives much of its support.

That is especially challenging because the United States, which would need to be one of Pakistan’s main backers, continues to strike targets in Pashtun areas, causing civilian casualties.
outputs.L3:
The Taliban has steadily expanded its influence inside Pakistan, particularly by moving northward along the border with Afghanistan and extending its presence into strategically important areas such as Swat and Buner. These advances have raised serious concerns because they show that Taliban-linked militants are no longer confined to remote tribal regions, but are increasingly able to project power into settled districts closer to Pakistan’s political and economic centers.

This expansion has been strengthened by the Taliban’s growing connections with Punjab-based terrorist groups. These links have allowed militants to broaden their operational reach and coordinate attacks beyond the border areas. Incidents such as the assault on a police station in Lahore illustrate how extremist networks based in different parts of Pakistan can cooperate, making the security threat more complex and more difficult for the state to contain.

The Pakistani government’s earlier approach to dealing with Taliban-linked groups has also contributed to the problem. Past agreements and cease-fire arrangements with militants, including deals that effectively ceded influence in certain areas, have often given these groups time and space to regroup, recruit, and expand. Rather than weakening the Taliban, such compromises have in some cases helped legitimize their authority and undermined the state’s ability to enforce the rule of law.

Despite these developments, Pakistan is unlikely to fall entirely under Taliban control. The country still has a powerful military, major urban centers, functioning political institutions, and a large population that does not broadly support Taliban rule. However, continued Taliban advances are deeply destabilizing. They place additional pressure on an already fragile government that faces political divisions, economic difficulties, and public frustration. Even limited Taliban gains can weaken confidence in the state and encourage further militant activity.

To address this challenge, Pakistan could pursue a broader political strategy in addition to military action. One possible response would be the formation of a national unity government that brings together major political parties and regional leaders behind a common plan to confront extremism. Such a government could help reduce internal political conflict and create a stronger national consensus. At the same time, Pakistan would benefit from greater international financial and trade support. Economic assistance, expanded market access, and development aid could help strengthen state institutions, create jobs, and reduce the conditions that allow extremist groups to gain influence. A combination of political unity, improved governance, security operations, and international support would give Pakistan a better chance of containing the Taliban’s expansion and stabilizing the country.

Taliban influence in Pakistan has expanded steadily in recent years, moving northward along the country’s long and porous border with Afghanistan and reaching beyond the tribal areas where the movement first established a strong presence. Its advance into districts such as Swat and Buner has shown that the group is no longer confined to remote frontier regions. Instead, it has been able to extend its reach into more settled areas, taking advantage of weak local administration, public frustration with corruption and slow justice, and the limited ability of the Pakistani state to enforce its authority consistently.

This expansion has not occurred in isolation. The Pakistani Taliban and related extremist factions have benefited from alliances with militant organizations based in Punjab, Pakistan’s most populous and politically important province. These alliances have allowed the Taliban to broaden its networks, gain access to new recruits and resources, and strengthen its capacity to operate outside its traditional base. In some cases, militants have also exploited government peace deals or ceasefire arrangements, using them not as a path toward stability but as an opportunity to regroup, impose their own authority, and push into nearby areas.

The situation in Swat illustrated the risks of such agreements. Deals that were intended to reduce violence instead gave militants room to consolidate control, enforce harsh interpretations of Islamic law, intimidate opponents, and challenge the state’s authority. The spread into Buner, closer to the capital Islamabad, raised particular alarm because it suggested that Taliban influence could move from the periphery toward Pakistan’s political heartland if left unchecked.

Despite these developments, Pakistan is not likely to fall to the Taliban. The country has a large military, functioning national institutions, major urban centers that remain outside Taliban control, and a population that is far from uniformly supportive of extremist rule. However, Taliban advances have placed additional strain on an already fragile and unstable government. Each territorial gain or successful challenge to state authority weakens public confidence, deepens political uncertainty, and makes it harder for civilian leaders to project control.

As a result, Pakistan faces a growing problem of volatility rather than an immediate collapse. The Taliban’s expansion undermines security, complicates relations between the government and the military, and increases pressure on political leaders to respond decisively. Even if the group cannot seize the country, its ability to destabilize key regions, influence local politics, and force concessions from the state could grow. In that sense, the Taliban’s advance represents a serious long-term challenge: not the imminent takeover of Pakistan, but the continued weakening of a state already struggling to maintain order and authority.

counterfactuals.output:
# Taliban advances in Pakistan: How their influence spread, whether the country could “fall,” and what comes next

Pakistan is facing a renewed militant threat from the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP — a separate but ideologically aligned group from the Afghan Taliban. The TTP has intensified attacks in recent years, particularly in Pakistan’s northwest, raising fears that militancy is again becoming entrenched in areas bordering Afghanistan.

The situation is not the same as Afghanistan’s 2021 collapse. Pakistan has a large military, a functioning state apparatus, nuclear weapons, major cities under government control and a political system — however turbulent — that is far more durable than the Afghan republic was in its final months. But the rise in TTP violence is a serious challenge for Islamabad, especially as Pakistan struggles with political polarization, economic stress and strained relations with the Taliban government in Kabul.

Below is a guide to what is happening, how the threat spread, and what options Pakistan and its partners have.

---

## What is the Pakistani Taliban?

The Pakistani Taliban, or TTP, is an umbrella militant organization formed in 2007 by factions operating mainly in Pakistan’s tribal belt along the Afghan border.

Its goals include overthrowing the Pakistani state, imposing its interpretation of Islamic law and expelling Pakistani security forces from areas it considers its strongholds. The TTP has carried out some of Pakistan’s deadliest attacks, including the 2014 massacre at the Army Public School in Peshawar, where more than 130 children were killed.

The TTP is distinct from the Afghan Taliban, which now rules Afghanistan. But the two movements share ideological roots, longstanding personal ties and overlapping networks. The Afghan Taliban’s return to power in Kabul in 2021 gave the TTP a major psychological and logistical boost.

---

## Where is the TTP strongest?

The TTP’s main activity is in northwestern Pakistan, especially Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province and districts along the Afghan border, including areas that were formerly part of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas, or FATA.

These areas have long been difficult for the Pakistani state to govern. Rugged terrain, cross-border tribal links, weak local institutions and years of war in Afghanistan have created openings for militant groups.

The TTP has also carried out attacks in Balochistan, Punjab and major cities, though it does not control large urban centers.

---

## How did Taliban influence spread in Pakistan?

Several factors helped the TTP regain momentum.

### 1. The Afghan Taliban’s victory changed the regional balance

When the Afghan Taliban took Kabul in August 2021, militant groups across the region viewed it as proof that an insurgency could defeat a state backed by major foreign powers.

For the TTP, the Afghan Taliban’s victory provided inspiration, sanctuary and breathing room. Many TTP fighters and leaders had been based in Afghanistan for years. With the Taliban in power there, Pakistan hoped Kabul would restrain or expel them. Instead, Islamabad says TTP fighters have continued to operate from Afghan soil — an allegation the Taliban government denies or downplays.

### 2. Failed ceasefires gave militants time to regroup

Pakistan held talks with the TTP after the Afghan Taliban takeover, including ceasefires that were meant to reduce violence. Critics say those pauses allowed militants to reorganize, recruit and re-enter parts of Pakistan.

The TTP formally ended a ceasefire in late 2022 and ordered attacks across the country. Since then, Pakistan has seen a sharp rise in assaults on police, soldiers and government installations.

### 3. Local grievances created openings

The TTP has exploited resentment in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa over insecurity, unemployment, displacement, corruption and heavy-handed military operations.

Many residents oppose both the militants and the state’s security tactics. In some communities, fear of Taliban reprisals has weakened cooperation with authorities. The TTP often uses intimidation — targeting tribal elders, police, informants and local officials — to expand influence without necessarily holding territory openly.

### 4. The border remains porous

Pakistan has built a fence along much of its frontier with Afghanistan, but the border remains difficult to control. Families, tribes and trade routes straddle both sides. Militants have used the terrain to move fighters, weapons and money.

### 5. Pakistan’s internal crises created distraction

Political turmoil, economic instability and tensions between civilian leaders and the military have absorbed attention in Islamabad. Militants tend to benefit when the state is divided or preoccupied.

---

## Is Pakistan at risk of falling to the Taliban?

A Taliban takeover of Pakistan is highly unlikely.

Pakistan is not Afghanistan in 2021. It has a far larger and more cohesive military, a more developed bureaucracy, major political parties, a larger economy and a powerful intelligence and security structure. The TTP does not command a national mass movement, and it faces strong resistance from many Pakistanis, including in Pashtun communities that have suffered heavily from militant violence.

However, “not falling” does not mean the threat is small.

The more realistic danger is a long-running insurgency that weakens state authority in border districts, increases attacks on security forces, scares away investment and fuels instability. If left unchecked, the TTP could expand its ability to extort businesses, assassinate local leaders, undermine policing and establish shadow influence in parts of the northwest.

That would not amount to seizing Islamabad, but it could still be deeply destabilizing.

---

## Could the TTP capture major cities?

Capturing and holding major cities such as Islamabad, Lahore, Karachi or Peshawar would be extremely difficult for the TTP.

Urban Pakistan is heavily policed and monitored, and the military has experience responding to militant attacks. The TTP can conduct bombings, assassinations and raids, but governing large cities would require manpower, logistics and public support it does not appear to have.

The greater risk is not urban conquest but urban terrorism — attacks designed to create fear, embarrass the government and show reach beyond the tribal areas.

---

## Why has Pakistan struggled to contain the threat?

Pakistan has fought the TTP before and pushed it out of several strongholds through large military operations, especially after 2014. But eliminating an insurgency is harder than clearing territory.

There are several challenges:

- **Cross-border sanctuary:** If militants can retreat into Afghanistan, Pakistani operations become less effective.  
- **Local policing gaps:** Military action can disrupt militants, but long-term security requires courts, police, schools, jobs and local governance.  
- **Militant adaptation:** The TTP has shifted from holding territory to guerrilla attacks, targeted killings and intimidation.  
- **Political inconsistency:** Negotiations, ceasefires and military campaigns have sometimes lacked continuity.  
- **Public mistrust:** Some communities fear both militants and security forces, making intelligence gathering harder.

---

## What role does Afghanistan’s Taliban government play?

This is one of the most sensitive questions.

Pakistan says the Afghan Taliban has not done enough to stop the TTP from operating out of Afghanistan. Islamabad has demanded action against TTP leaders, training camps and safe havens.

The Taliban government in Kabul has rejected accusations that it is allowing attacks on Pakistan and says Pakistan’s security problems are domestic. It has also resisted strong action against the TTP, partly because many TTP members fought alongside the Afghan Taliban during the war against the US-backed Afghan government.

Kabul faces a dilemma: cracking down on the TTP could create internal divisions and push some militants toward more extreme groups such as ISIS-K. But refusing to act risks a deteriorating relationship with Pakistan, one of Afghanistan’s most important neighbors.

---

## What can Pakistan do?

Pakistan has several options, though none is easy.

### 1. Strengthen local security and policing

A sustainable counterinsurgency cannot rely only on the army. Pakistan needs stronger local police, intelligence networks, prosecutors and courts in vulnerable districts.

That means protecting police stations, improving training, paying officers reliably and ensuring local communities trust law enforcement enough to share information.

### 2. Avoid repeating failed deals

Negotiations with insurgents are not inherently wrong, but past deals with the TTP often allowed militants to regroup. Any future talks would need strict conditions, verifiable enforcement and broad political consensus.

A ceasefire that gives militants time and space without disarmament or accountability could worsen the threat.

### 3. Improve governance in former tribal areas

The merger of former FATA into Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was meant to bring constitutional rights, courts and development to the region. Many residents say the promises have not been fully delivered.

Better roads, schools, hospitals, jobs, compensation for war damage and responsive local administration would reduce the space militants exploit.

### 4. Use targeted military pressure

Pakistan is likely to continue intelligence-based operations against TTP commanders and cells. Large-scale military offensives may be used if militants seize territory, but they risk civilian displacement and backlash.

The key is precision: degrading militant networks while avoiding tactics that alienate local populations.

### 5. Manage relations with Kabul

Pakistan has tried pressure, diplomacy and border restrictions to push the Afghan Taliban to act against the TTP. Islamabad may continue combining incentives and coercion.

But the relationship is complicated. Heavy-handed border closures can hurt ordinary Afghans and Pakistan’s own trade interests, while airstrikes or cross-border actions risk escalation.

---

## What can the international community do?

The international community has limited leverage, but it is not powerless.

### 1. Support counterterrorism capacity

Countries with an interest in regional stability can help Pakistan improve border security, forensic investigations, police training and financial tracking of militant networks.

This support is most effective when focused on civilian law enforcement and accountability, not just military hardware.

### 2. Pressure the Afghan Taliban

Regional powers — including China, Iran, Central Asian states, Gulf countries and Western governments — can press Kabul to prevent Afghan territory from being used by transnational militants.

The challenge is coordination. Many governments engage the Taliban for practical reasons but do not recognize it formally. That gives them some leverage, but it is fragmented.

### 3. Tie engagement with Kabul to counterterrorism benchmarks

Humanitarian aid should not be politicized, but diplomatic engagement, sanctions relief and economic access can be linked to measurable counterterrorism steps, such as restricting militant movement and preventing training camps.

### 4. Help stabilize Pakistan economically

Economic crisis can weaken a state’s ability to fight militancy. International financial support, debt relief discussions and investment can indirectly improve security by reducing instability — though such assistance often comes with difficult reform conditions.

### 5. Prevent regional spillover

The TTP threat overlaps with wider concerns about ISIS-K, al Qaeda remnants, sectarian militants and separatist violence. Regional intelligence-sharing could help prevent attacks beyond Pakistan’s borders.

---

## What happens next?

Pakistan is likely to face continued militant violence, particularly against police, soldiers and government targets in the northwest. The TTP may try to expand its influence through targeted killings, extortion and propaganda rather than open territorial conquest.

A decisive Taliban-style march on Islamabad is improbable. But a grinding insurgency could still impose heavy costs: weakening local governance, straining the military, discouraging investment and deepening public fear.

The outcome will depend on whether Pakistan can combine security operations with credible governance — and whether the Afghan Taliban decides, or is pressured, to curb the TTP’s use of Afghan territory.

For now, Pakistan’s challenge is not state collapse. It is preventing a persistent insurgency from becoming a permanent feature of national life.

counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write a piece falsely attributed to CNN’s Nic Robertson, but here is an original news analysis on the same subject:

---

## Taliban’s Growing Influence in Pakistan Poses New Risks for Islamabad and Washington

Pakistan’s long, complicated relationship with the Taliban is entering a more dangerous phase. What was once viewed by parts of Pakistan’s security establishment as strategic leverage in Afghanistan is increasingly becoming a direct threat at home — and a growing concern for Washington.

Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, militant networks operating along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border have gained confidence, mobility and ideological momentum. Chief among them is the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, a Pakistani Taliban movement that has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians.

Islamabad has repeatedly accused Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers of allowing the TTP to operate from Afghan territory. The Taliban government denies providing sanctuary, but Pakistan says cross-border militancy has become harder to contain since the collapse of the former Afghan republic and the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.

For Pakistan, the risk is both immediate and structural. The country is already facing economic stress, political instability and tensions between civilian leaders and the military. A renewed insurgency in the northwest could stretch the state’s capacity at a time when public trust in institutions is fragile.

The Taliban’s ideological pull also presents a broader challenge. Even if Afghan Taliban leaders do not directly command Pakistani militants, their victory over a US-backed government has energized extremist groups across the region. The message is simple and potent: persistence can defeat a powerful state.

That perception matters in Pakistan’s border provinces, where communities have endured years of military operations, displacement and militant violence. If Islamabad responds with heavy-handed tactics, it risks alienating local populations. If it responds too softly, militants may consolidate.

For Washington, the dilemma is different but connected. The United States no longer has troops in Afghanistan, but it still has counterterrorism interests in the region. Groups such as ISIS-K remain a concern, while al Qaeda’s long-standing ties to Taliban factions continue to worry US officials.

Pakistan has historically been a critical, if difficult, counterterrorism partner for Washington. But cooperation has been strained by mistrust, shifting regional priorities and Pakistan’s own domestic turmoil. The US needs intelligence access and regional stability; Pakistan wants security assistance, diplomatic relevance and relief from economic pressure.

The growing strength of Taliban-aligned militancy complicates both agendas. If Pakistan becomes more unstable, Washington’s ability to monitor threats from Afghanistan could weaken. If Pakistan conducts cross-border strikes or escalates pressure on Kabul, the region could see a dangerous cycle of retaliation.

There is also a nuclear dimension. Pakistan’s nuclear arsenal is secure by most expert assessments, but rising militancy in a nuclear-armed state inevitably attracts global attention. The concern is not imminent loss of control, but the compounding effect of political chaos, extremist violence and institutional strain.

Islamabad’s options are limited. It can pressure the Afghan Taliban diplomatically, use military force along the border, pursue talks with the TTP, or attempt some combination of all three. Each path carries risks. Negotiations may embolden militants. Military action may provoke backlash. Diplomatic pressure may have little effect if Kabul is unwilling or unable to restrain allied factions.

The deeper problem is that Pakistan’s historic distinction between “good” and “bad” militants has become increasingly untenable. Groups once seen as tools of influence can splinter, merge or turn inward. The Taliban’s success in Afghanistan has shifted the balance of confidence toward non-state actors.

For Washington, the lesson is equally stark. Leaving Afghanistan did not end the region’s security problems; it changed the tools available to manage them. The US now has fewer eyes on the ground, less leverage over Kabul and a more complicated relationship with Islamabad.

The Taliban’s growing influence in Pakistan is not a single crisis but an accumulation of pressures: border insecurity, ideological radicalization, economic fragility and geopolitical mistrust. If left unmanaged, it could destabilize Pakistan further, embolden extremist networks and force Washington back into a region it hoped to deprioritize.

The danger for Islamabad is that the militancy it once believed it could contain may now be shaping the state’s security agenda. The danger for Washington is that distance may no longer be enough to keep Afghanistan and Pakistan’s instability from becoming an international threat again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the situation in Pakistan as the Taliban expands from the tribal border areas into Swat and Buner, explaining the causes, political implications, and possible policy responses.
counterfactuals.output:
The Taliban’s expansion from Pakistan’s tribal border areas into Swat and Buner represents a serious challenge to the Pakistani state, not merely a local security problem. It suggests that militant groups once concentrated in the Federally Administered Tribal Areas are exploiting weak governance, public frustration, and political hesitation to extend their influence into settled areas closer to the country’s core.

### Causes

Several factors help explain the Taliban’s advance:

- **Weak state presence and poor governance:** In areas such as Swat, many residents had long complained about slow courts, corruption, abusive local elites, and ineffective administration. Taliban promises of “quick justice” gained traction where the state was seen as absent or predatory.

- **Aftermath of Afghan war dynamics:** Militancy in Pakistan is tied to the conflict in Afghanistan. Cross-border networks, ideological affinity, and the legacy of Pakistan’s past support for jihadist groups helped create an environment in which armed Islamist movements could organize and expand.

- **Military and political inconsistency:** Pakistan’s security establishment has often alternated between offensives, ceasefires, and peace deals. Agreements with militants—such as arrangements in Swat allowing some form of Islamic law—were intended to buy peace but often gave the Taliban time and legitimacy to regroup.

- **Public fear and coercion:** Taliban influence is not simply the result of popular support. Militants have used intimidation, executions, destruction of schools, and attacks on opponents to silence resistance.

- **Economic distress:** Poverty, unemployment, and lack of services made young men more vulnerable to recruitment and made communities less able to resist armed groups.

### Political implications

The Taliban’s movement into Swat and Buner alarmed Pakistanis because these areas are far beyond the remote tribal belt and relatively close to Islamabad. The advance raised doubts about the state’s capacity and willingness to defend its territory.

Politically, it put pressure on Pakistan’s civilian government and military leadership. The government faced criticism for appearing to concede authority to militants, while the army faced demands to act decisively. It also sharpened tensions between Pakistan and the United States, since Washington saw Taliban sanctuaries in Pakistan as a direct threat to the war effort in Afghanistan.

Domestically, the crisis exposed a broader ideological divide: some political and religious forces viewed negotiations with militants as necessary or even legitimate, while others warned that compromise would embolden extremists and undermine Pakistan’s constitutional order.

The situation also had international implications. Pakistan is a nuclear-armed state, so any sign that extremist groups are expanding unchecked creates anxiety among regional and global powers.

### Possible policy responses

A durable response would require more than military action alone.

- **Targeted security operations:** The state may need to clear militant-held areas, protect population centers, and prevent further expansion. But operations must be disciplined to avoid civilian casualties that could fuel more resentment.

- **Hold and govern after clearing:** Military gains will not last unless police, courts, schools, health services, and local administration return quickly. The state must show that it can provide justice and security better than the Taliban.

- **Judicial and administrative reform:** Since militant groups exploit frustration with corrupt or slow institutions, Pakistan needs faster courts, accountable policing, and functioning local government.

- **Political consensus:** Civilian leaders, the military, and major parties need a shared position that armed groups cannot be allowed to impose rule by force. Ambiguous distinctions between “good” and “bad” militants weaken the response.

- **Economic development:** Reconstruction, jobs, education, and compensation for displaced families are essential to reduce Taliban recruitment and restore public confidence.

- **Control of militant financing and propaganda:** Authorities need to disrupt funding networks, illegal FM radio broadcasts, intimidation campaigns, and recruitment pipelines.

- **Regional coordination:** Pakistan’s approach must be linked to Afghanistan policy, border management, and cooperation with international partners, while also addressing Pakistani concerns about sovereignty and civilian harm from foreign military actions.

In short, the Taliban’s expansion into Swat and Buner reflects a combination of state weakness, militant coercion, failed peace deals, and social grievances. The central political question is whether Pakistan can build a coherent national strategy that combines force with governance reform. Without that, any temporary military victory risks being followed by another militant resurgence.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN report beginning “(CNN) -- Taliban advances in Pakistan are raising concerns…” and include discussion of Punjab militant groups, government deals with the Taliban, India-Pakistan tensions, and U.S. strikes in Pashtun areas.
counterfactuals.output:
(CNN) -- Taliban advances in Pakistan are raising concerns among officials and analysts who warn that militant gains in the country’s northwest could deepen instability, embolden extremist networks in Punjab and further strain relations between Islamabad, New Delhi and Washington.

Pakistani authorities have faced mounting pressure as Taliban-linked fighters expand influence beyond traditional strongholds in the Pashtun tribal belt and parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The movement’s reach has raised fears that militant factions could exploit weak governance, local grievances and past peace agreements to consolidate power.

A particular concern for security officials is the relationship between the Pakistani Taliban and militant organizations based in Punjab, the country’s most populous province and political heartland. Punjab has long been home to sectarian and anti-India militant groups, some of which analysts say have provided recruits, logistics or ideological support to insurgents fighting the state. The potential for cooperation between Pashtun Taliban fighters and Punjab-based extremist networks could broaden the insurgency’s geographic and operational scope.

The Pakistani government has at times pursued deals with Taliban factions, arguing that negotiations can reduce violence and restore order in areas where the military has struggled to maintain control. Critics say such agreements have often allowed militants to regroup, impose harsh interpretations of Islamic law and expand their influence while the state retreats.

The unrest also intersects with tensions between India and Pakistan. New Delhi has repeatedly accused Pakistan-based militant groups of involvement in attacks on Indian targets, while Islamabad denies supporting terrorism and says it is itself a victim of militant violence. Any major attack linked to Pakistan-based groups could quickly escalate diplomatic and military tensions between the nuclear-armed neighbors.

Meanwhile, U.S. strikes targeting al Qaeda and Taliban figures in Pashtun areas along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border have added another layer of complexity. Washington has viewed the region as a haven for militants plotting attacks in Afghanistan and beyond. But the strikes have fueled anger inside Pakistan, where many see them as violations of sovereignty and a source of civilian casualties, even as U.S. officials argue they are necessary to disrupt extremist networks.

The challenge for Pakistan, analysts say, is balancing military action, political negotiation and regional diplomacy while preventing militant groups from exploiting divisions between the central government, provincial authorities and the security establishment.

“The danger is not just that the Taliban gains territory,” one regional security analyst said. “It is that different militant networks begin to reinforce one another — in the tribal areas, in Punjab and across the wider region.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a Q&A news article about whether Pakistan is at risk of failing due to Taliban advances, what role the Pakistani government’s past deals played, and how foreign governments could help stabilize the country.
counterfactuals.output:
# Is Pakistan at risk of failing as Taliban violence spreads? A Q&A on the crisis, past deals and foreign help

**By [News Desk]**

Pakistan is facing renewed concern over militant violence, particularly from the Pakistani Taliban, known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan or TTP. Attacks on police, soldiers and civilians have raised questions about whether the country’s security institutions can contain the threat — and whether past efforts to negotiate with militants helped strengthen them.

Below is a Q&A explaining the risks, the role of previous government deals and what foreign governments can do to help stabilize Pakistan.

---

## Is Pakistan at risk of “failing” because of Taliban advances?

Pakistan is under serious pressure, but most analysts would not describe it as on the brink of state failure.

The country still has a large and organized military, functioning federal institutions, a national tax system, courts, provincial governments and a powerful security apparatus. Unlike a fully failing state, Pakistan’s central government has not lost control of the capital or the core instruments of state power.

However, the risk is not imaginary. Pakistan faces overlapping crises: militant attacks, political polarization, economic distress, climate shocks, ethnic and sectarian tensions, and strained relations with Afghanistan. These pressures can weaken state capacity even if the state does not collapse.

The areas of greatest concern are along the Afghan border, especially parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and former tribal regions, where militants have historically found sanctuary, local support networks and difficult terrain. Balochistan also faces a separate insurgency, along with sectarian and extremist violence.

The danger is less a sudden national collapse and more a gradual erosion of government authority in specific regions — with militants able to intimidate local officials, attack security forces, collect funds, assassinate opponents and disrupt daily life.

---

## Who are the Taliban groups involved?

There are two distinct but related groups that often cause confusion.

The **Afghan Taliban** rule Afghanistan after taking power in Kabul in 2021. They are primarily focused on Afghanistan, though their victory inspired militants across the region.

The **Pakistani Taliban**, or **TTP**, are a separate insurgent coalition that seeks to overthrow or weaken the Pakistani state and impose its version of Islamic rule. The TTP has carried out some of Pakistan’s deadliest attacks, including assaults on schools, mosques, police stations, military facilities and political gatherings.

Pakistan says TTP fighters operate from sanctuaries in Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban deny allowing Afghan soil to be used for attacks, but Pakistan and many outside observers say Kabul has either been unwilling or unable to fully restrain the group.

---

## What changed after the Afghan Taliban returned to power?

The Afghan Taliban’s takeover altered the regional balance.

For years, Pakistani officials believed that a friendly or at least non-hostile government in Kabul would improve Pakistan’s security. Instead, the TTP gained morale, space and, according to Pakistani officials, increased cross-border freedom.

The fall of the U.S.-backed Afghan government also released prisoners, shifted weapons around the region and boosted the prestige of jihadist groups. The TTP used this momentum to reorganize, absorb splinter factions and intensify attacks inside Pakistan.

The result has been a major security reversal for Islamabad: a Taliban-led Afghanistan has not delivered the border stability Pakistan hoped for.

---

## Did Pakistan’s past deals with militants contribute to the problem?

Yes, many security experts argue that past peace deals helped militants regroup, though the picture is complicated.

Successive Pakistani governments and military authorities have struck agreements with militant groups in tribal areas and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa over the past two decades. These deals were often intended to reduce violence quickly, free hostages, avoid costly military operations or divide militant factions.

But many agreements were criticized because they allowed militants to retain weapons, impose parallel authority, gain time to recruit and rearm, and present themselves as legitimate power brokers. In some cases, militants used ceasefires to consolidate control before resuming attacks.

Critics say the state repeatedly traded short-term calm for long-term insecurity.

---

## Why did Pakistani governments make those deals?

Officials often faced difficult choices. Military operations in border regions were costly, displaced civilians and created political backlash. Local administrations were weak, and the terrain favored insurgents. Negotiations sometimes appeared to be the fastest way to stop bloodshed.

There was also a long-running debate inside Pakistan’s establishment about distinguishing between militant groups that attacked Pakistan and those focused on Afghanistan or India. Critics say that selective approach created space for extremist networks to survive and overlap.

In recent years, Pakistani leaders have increasingly acknowledged that tolerating or bargaining with some militant groups can backfire. But dismantling those networks is difficult, particularly when they have local roots, ideological support, criminal financing and cross-border links.

---

## Were the talks with the TTP after 2021 a mistake?

Many Pakistani politicians, security officials and civil society groups now say the post-2021 talks with the TTP were deeply flawed.

Those negotiations, reportedly mediated in part by the Afghan Taliban, led to ceasefires and discussions about allowing some militants to return to Pakistan. Opponents warned that this would let hardened fighters re-enter communities they had previously terrorized.

The ceasefire eventually collapsed, and the TTP resumed attacks. Critics argue the process gave the group time to regroup and relocate, while undermining public confidence in the state.

Supporters of talks said dialogue was worth attempting if it could split militants or reduce violence. But the failure of the ceasefire strengthened the argument that negotiations without disarmament, accountability and state control are dangerous.

---

## Could Pakistan’s nuclear weapons be at risk?

There is no public evidence that Pakistan’s nuclear arsenal is at immediate risk from Taliban militants.

Pakistan’s nuclear weapons are believed to be controlled by a heavily guarded command-and-control system under the military. Foreign governments, especially the United States, have long monitored the issue closely.

That said, instability in a nuclear-armed country is always a major international concern. The more Pakistan faces internal violence, political chaos and economic stress, the more foreign governments worry about crisis management, extremist infiltration, regional escalation and command security.

The greater near-term risk is not militants seizing nuclear weapons, but instability leading to miscalculation, weakened governance or conflict with neighbors.

---

## What role does Pakistan’s economy play in the security crisis?

A major one.

Economic hardship can fuel instability by increasing unemployment, weakening public services and reducing the government’s ability to invest in policing, courts, education and development. Inflation and debt pressures also damage public trust in the state.

Militant groups often exploit areas where the government is absent or predatory. If citizens cannot rely on the state for security, justice or basic services, armed groups can gain influence by intimidation or by presenting themselves as alternatives.

Stabilizing Pakistan therefore requires more than military operations. It requires economic reform, local governance, education, infrastructure and credible justice.

---

## How can foreign governments help stabilize Pakistan?

Foreign governments can help, but they cannot solve Pakistan’s internal security problems on their own. Assistance is most useful when it strengthens civilian institutions, improves border security and supports economic resilience without empowering abusive practices.

Possible steps include:

### 1. Support economic stabilization  
International lenders and partner countries can help Pakistan manage debt, maintain essential imports and avoid balance-of-payments crises. But aid is more effective when tied to transparent reforms, tax collection, anti-corruption measures and social protection for the poor.

### 2. Strengthen police and civilian law enforcement  
Pakistan’s military is powerful, but long-term counterterrorism depends on capable local police, prosecutors, judges and intelligence coordination. Foreign training and funding can help improve forensic capacity, community policing, witness protection and court processes.

### 3. Improve border management  
Pakistan and Afghanistan share a long, difficult border. Technical support for surveillance, legal crossings, customs systems and biometric controls could help reduce militant movement while keeping trade and humanitarian traffic open.

### 4. Encourage Pakistan-Afghanistan dialogue  
Outside powers, including China, Gulf states, the United States and regional organizations, can press Kabul and Islamabad to maintain communication and avoid escalation. The goal would be to reduce cross-border attacks, share intelligence and prevent refugee and trade disputes from becoming security crises.

### 5. Provide development aid to vulnerable regions  
Militant influence grows where the state is absent. Targeted investment in schools, clinics, roads, water systems and local jobs in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, former tribal districts and Balochistan can reduce recruitment and improve trust in the government.

### 6. Avoid backing short-term militant bargains  
Foreign governments should discourage deals that allow armed groups to keep weapons, run parallel courts or control territory. Negotiations, if they occur, should require disarmament, reintegration monitoring and protection for local communities.

### 7. Help with refugee and humanitarian pressures  
Pakistan hosts large numbers of Afghans and has periodically moved to expel undocumented migrants, creating humanitarian and diplomatic strains. International funding for refugees, host communities and legal processing could reduce pressure on Pakistan while protecting vulnerable people.

---

## What should foreign governments avoid?

They should avoid seeing Pakistan only through a counterterrorism lens.

Heavy-handed security assistance without accountability can deepen grievances. Publicly humiliating Pakistan can fuel nationalist backlash. Ignoring human rights abuses, enforced disappearances or political repression can make long-term stability harder.

Foreign governments should also avoid assuming that Pakistan’s military alone can deliver stability. The country’s resilience depends on civilian governance, political legitimacy and economic opportunity.

---

## What does Pakistan need to do internally?

Pakistan’s most urgent task is to restore a consistent state policy toward militancy: no armed group should be allowed to operate as a proxy, political enforcer or “negotiating partner” while retaining coercive power.

The government also needs to rebuild public confidence in regions affected by militancy. That means protecting local leaders, compensating victims, supporting displaced families and ensuring that counterterrorism operations do not punish entire communities.

Political stability matters as well. Persistent confrontation among political parties, courts, the military and civilian authorities distracts from security threats and weakens the state’s legitimacy.

---

## Bottom line: Is Pakistan likely to fail?

Pakistan is not likely to collapse in the near term. Its military and state institutions remain far stronger than those of countries typically described as failed states.

But parts of the country face a real risk of worsening militant control and chronic insecurity if the TTP continues expanding, if Afghanistan remains a sanctuary, and if Pakistan relies on temporary deals rather than durable governance.

Foreign help can reduce the pressure, especially through economic support, policing assistance and diplomacy with Afghanistan. But the decisive choices will be Pakistan’s: whether it can end ambiguous policies toward militants, strengthen civilian institutions and deliver security and services to citizens in the areas most at risk.
